title: Euler's descent: a small multiple of a prime that is a sum of two squares descends to the prime
statement: Let p be prime (2 <= p, and every divisor of p is 1 or p). If for some natural n with 0 < n < p the multiple n*p is a sum of two integer squares, then p ITSELF is a sum of two integer squares. This is Euler's infinite descent, by strong induction on the multiplier n.

formal.statement: theorem Int.exists_sum_of_two_squares_of_multiple : ((x0 : AxNat) -> ((x1 : And (AxNat.le (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) x0) (((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : AxNat.dvd x1 x0) -> Or (Eq.{1} AxNat x1 (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) (Eq.{1} AxNat x1 x0))))) -> ((x2 : AxNat) -> ((x3 : AxNat.lt AxNat.zero x2) -> ((x4 : AxNat.lt x2 x0) -> ((x5 : Exists.{1} Int (fun (x5 : Int) => Exists.{1} Int (fun (x6 : Int) => Eq.{1} Int (Int.mul (Int.ofNat x2) (Int.ofNat x0)) (Int.add (Int.mul x5 x5) (Int.mul x6 x6))))) -> Int.IsSumOfTwoSquares (Int.ofNat x0)))))))

notes: The third of ADR-1647's four pieces, and the one that fixes the shape of the whole proof. THE MULTIPLIER IS QUANTIFIED AS Int.ofNat n OVER A Nat INDEX, not as an Int m carrying a natAbs m = n bridge hypothesis. Int.le/Int.lt at two ofNat's is DEFINITIONALLY the corresponding Nat relation (order_coercion.rs proves both its lemmas by fun h => h), so in this spelling 0 < m, m < p and 1 < m are the Nat hypotheses themselves, and the whole proof contains exactly ONE transport across of_nat_nat_abs_of_nonneg -- at the recursive call, where the new multiplier q genuinely arrives as an Int with 0 <= q < m. The bridge spelling would have needed three transports at every level of the recursion AND would have had to re-establish the bridge at the recursive call anyway. A second consequence: no refl-generalisation of the motive is needed. Nat.Hall.hall_sufficient, the other Prop-motive user of Nat.strongInduction here, must state its motive as (forall s nb, card s = n -> ...) and apply it at card s with Eq.refl, because its measure is a FUNCTION OF its subject; here the measure IS the index. Base case n = 1: the multiple is the prime itself. Inductive case 1 < n: centre both squares modulo m, produce the next multiplier, bound it, rule out q = 0, and hand Int.descentStep's output to the induction hypothesis at natAbs q.
